PMF IAS – Learn Smart 67 x Kepler’s Third Law: The square of the orbital period of a planet is proportional to the cube of the semi- major axis of its orbit. Hankwang, Wikipedia Orbital period (T): time taken by a plant to complete one revolution around the sun. Semi Major Axis (a1 and a2): half of the major axis of the ellipse. T12/a13 = T22/a23 x In simple terms, the distance of a planet from the sun determines the time it takes for that planet to revolve around the sun (farther the planet is, greater the orbital period). Planet Orbital Period (T) in years Average Distance (R) in AU T2/R3 Mercury 0.241 0.39 0.98 Venus .615 0.72 1.01 Earth 1.00 1.00 1.00 Mars 1.88 1.52 1.01 Perigee and Apogee x Most satellites orbit the earth in elliptical patterns. x When a satellite is at its farthest point from the earth, it is at the apogee of the orbit. x When a satellite is at its closest point to the earth, it is at the perigee of the orbit. x In accordance with Kepler’s second law, the satellites are fastest at the perigee and slowest at the apogee. -0 . - →÷% : de PMF IAS – Learn Smart 68 Why satellites revolve rather than staying still in space? x There are two important forces acting on the satellite: 1) the gravitational force which will pull the satellite towards earth and 2) the centrifugal force (due to revolution) which counters the gravitational pull. Source x Revolution causes centrifugal force (the object tends to move away from the centre). x Higher the speed of the revolving satellite (orbital velocity), higher the centrifugal force. x Thus, by varying the speed (orbital velocity) of the satellite, we can make the satellite 1) fall back to earth by decreasing the orbital velocity (centrifugal force < gravitational force) 2) stay in its orbit by adjusting the speed so that the centrifugal force balances the gravitational pull (centrifugal force = gravitational force). (Lower the orbit, higher should be the orbital velocity). 3) escape earth’s influence by keeping the orbital velocity above the required speed (centrifugal force > gravitational force). Low Earth Orbit (LEO: 200-2000 km) & PMF IAS – Learn Smart 69 x International Space Station (400 km), the Hubble Space Telescope (560 km) and some observation sat- ellites are all rotating the earth in Low Earth Orbit. x LEO is high enough to significantly reduce the atmospheric drag yet close enough to observe the earth (re- mote sensing). x In LEO, the satellite’s orbital period is much smaller than the earth’s rotational period (24 hours). x That is, the satellites in LEO complete multiple revolutions in 24 hours (Lower the orbit, higher should be the speed). Source What is the speed required to keep a satellite in LEO? x The speed is dependent on the distance from the centre of the Earth. x At an altitude of 200 km, the required orbital velocity is a little more than 27,400 kmph. x In the case of the space shuttle, it orbits the Earth once every 90 minutes at an altitude of 466 km. Advantages of LEO x Low Earth Orbit is used for things that we want to visit often, like the International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope and some satellites (usually spy satellites and other observation satellites). x This is convenient for installing new instruments, experiments, and return to earth in a relatively short time. Disadvantages of LEO x Atmospheric drag will lead to more fuel consumption and constant speed adjustments. ↳air friction due to atmosphere . PMF IAS – Learn Smart 70 x A satellite traveling in LEO do not spend very long over any one part of the Earth at a given time. x Hence, satellites in LEO are not suitable for communication and weather observation and forecasting. Solution x One solution is to put a satellite in a highly elliptical orbit (eccentric orbit ― non-geosynchronous). x The other is to place the satellite in a geosynchronous orbit. Highly Elliptical Orbits x Kepler's second law: an object in orbit about Earth moves much faster when it is close to Earth than when it is farther away. x Perigee is the closest point and apogee is the farthest. x If the orbit is very elliptical, the satellite will spend most of its time near apogee (the furthest point in its orbit) where it moves very slowly. x Thus, it can be above a specific location most of the time. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 71 Disadvantages of Highly Elliptical Orbits x In a highly elliptical orbit, the satellite has long dwell time over one area, but at certain times when the satellite is on the high speed portion of the orbit, there is no coverage over the desired area. Solution x We could have two satellites on similar orbits but timed to be on opposite sides at any given time. x In this way, there will always be one satellite over the desired coverage area at all times. x If we want continuous coverage over the entire planet at all times, such as the Global Positioning System (GPS satellites are in Medium Earth Orbit though), then we must have a constellation of satellites with orbits that are both different in location and time. x In this way, there is a satellite over every part of the Earth at any given time. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 72 Satellite constellation (Source) Geosynchronous Orbits (GSO) x Another solution to the dwell time problem is to have a satellite whose orbital period is equal to the period of rotation of the earth (24 hrs) (satellite’s revolution is in sync with the earth’s rotation). x In this case, the satellite cannot be too close to the Earth because it would not be going fast enough to counteract the pull of gravity. x Using Kepler's third law it is determined that the satellite has to be placed approximately 36,000 km away from the surface of the Earth (~42,000 km from the centre of the Earth) in order to remain in a GSO orbit. x By positioning a satellite so that it has infinite dwell time over one spot on the Earth, we can constantly monitor the weather in one location, provide reliable telecommunications service, etc. x The downside of a GSO is that it is more expensive to put and maintain something that high up. Geostationary Orbit or Geosynchronous Equatorial Orbit (GEO) x A geostationary orbit or geosynchronous equatorial orbit is a circular geosynchronous orbit above Earth's equator and following the direction of Earth's rotation. x Because the satellite stays right over the same spot all the time, this kind of orbit is called "geostationary."
